Where does HCV linkage break down?
A community buprenorphine cohort from Taiwan

This Taiwan cohort raises a practical question for HCV elimination: when screening or reassessment identifies a need for care, what prevents patients from reaching diagnostic confirmation? The largest observed loss occurred before hospital assessment, but the study was not designed to establish a single cause.

Why the Taiwan context matters

A different treatment setting may create a different linkage problem.

In Taiwan, HCV elimination efforts have included methadone programs and correctional settings. Buprenorphine/naloxone treatment operates differently, with periodic visits, take-home dosing, and delivery across hospital and community settings. This makes community BPN care a useful setting for asking whether the usual screening-to-treatment pathway depends too heavily on patients crossing into another service system.

01 · TAIWAN SERVICE SETTING

Community BPN clinics

Outreach was embedded in community buprenorphine/naloxone treatment settings in Taoyuan, linking addiction care with HCV screening history and treatment needs.

02 · SCREEN / REASSESS

HCV status and care-history review

Never-screened participants received rapid anti-HCV testing. Participants with known HCV history were reassessed when current viraemia or follow-up status still needed clarification.

03 · LINKAGE

Case-manager supported referral

Referral to Taoyuan General Hospital enabled RNA assessment and DAA treatment when indicated.

Linkage to hospital HCV care

Agreement to referral was not the same as attendance.

Among 46 participants needing further evaluation, 27 accepted referral and 20 completed hospital assessment. In this Taiwan community BPN cohort, the largest observed loss occurred before diagnostic confirmation at the referral hospital.

UNADJUSTED COMPARISONS
Sexp = 0.0159
Willing participants included more women; all 19 unwilling participants were male. This was an unadjusted comparison.
First heroin injection agep = 0.0438
A younger age at first heroin injection was more common among those willing to accept referral.
BPN dosep = 0.0118
Mean BPN dose was higher among willing participants (4.23 ± 2.34 mg vs 2.70 ± 1.55 mg). Dose was not a direct measure of adherence.
Distance to referral hospitalp = 0.0152
Participants living farther from the referral hospital appeared less willing to accept referral.
The adjusted model found no statistically significant associations; estimates were imprecise. These signals should not be interpreted as independent determinants or causes.
Discussion · what might explain the gap?

The data identify where people were lost. They do not yet tell us why.

Rather than treating the cascade as proof of one intervention, we use it to generate competing explanations. Open each question below to see what the current data support — and what would still need to be measured.

QUESTION 01 · ACCESS

Is cross-hospital referral itself the barrier?

Distance was associated with referral willingness in unadjusted comparison, and 7 participants accepted referral but still did not attend.

What remains unknown?

Travel time, transport cost, appointment availability, work constraints, competing care demands, and whether near-site RNA testing would actually improve attendance were not directly measured.

QUESTION 02 · READINESS

Is “willingness” too simple a measure?

Referral acceptance captured a decision at one moment, but acceptance did not guarantee hospital attendance.

What remains unknown?

Perceived need, HCV knowledge, fear of diagnosis, stigma, prior healthcare experiences, treatment priorities, and changes in motivation between referral and appointment were incompletely characterized.

QUESTION 03 · SERVICE MODEL

Does BPN care create a distinct engagement pattern?

Community BPN treatment can involve periodic visits and take-home medication, unlike daily supervised methadone dosing.

What remains unknown?

This study had no contemporary methadone comparator, so it cannot determine whether the observed linkage pattern is specific to BPN, to community treatment, or to this local referral pathway.

QUESTION 04 · CARE DESIGN

Would decentralizing RNA testing change the cascade?

The observed losses occur before diagnostic confirmation, making on-site or near-site RNA assessment a plausible service redesign to test.

Why is this still a hypothesis?

No on-site RNA comparison was included. A prospective implementation study would be needed to test whether decentralization improves completion, time to diagnosis, treatment initiation, and cost.

QUESTION 05 · CASE MANAGEMENT

What did case management solve — and what could it not solve?

Case managers supported referral, yet 19 declined and 7 did not attend after accepting.

What should be measured next?

Type and intensity of navigation support, number of contacts, reasons for refusal or non-attendance, rescheduling, accompaniment, and whether specific supports change completion rates.

QUESTION 06 · GENERALIZABILITY

Is this a Taiwan-wide issue or a local signal?

The cohort came from a local outreach program in Taoyuan and should not be treated as representative of all people receiving BPN in Taiwan.

What would strengthen inference?

Replication across regions, larger samples, clearer denominators for the BPN population, and comparison across clinic types and referral models.

The most useful interpretation may be a question rather than a conclusion: how much of the HCV cascade is a clinical problem, and how much is a service-design problem?

LIMITATION

Local outreach sample

Findings should not be generalized directly to all people receiving BPN in Taiwan.

LIMITATION

Exploratory referral analysis

Small samples, sparse groups and multiple comparisons limit inference; the adjusted model found no statistically significant associations.

LIMITATION

Missing reasons behind attrition

Reasons for refusal and non-attendance were incompletely characterized, and treatment follow-up remained ongoing.

INHSU 2026 poster

Challenges in linkage to HCV care among patients receiving BPN in Taiwan.

The poster presents the observed cascade. This interactive version is designed to support discussion about what the losses may mean, what remains uncertain, and which questions should be tested next.

  • Setting: community buprenorphine/naloxone treatment clinics in Taoyuan, Taiwan.
  • Participants: 90 people receiving BPN; 42 had never been screened for HCV.
  • Linkage cohort: 46 required further evaluation; 20 completed hospital assessment.
  • Treatment: all 9 participants with detectable HCV RNA initiated DAA treatment.
